entry.title: Time Series Analysis
entry.content:
Usually, it makes sense to consider the data as a random sample; i.e. independent and identically distributed. Then one can model the distribution and do testing, confidence intervals, or regressions.

But in the case of data ordered in time, say intraday stock prices, the points in the sample are often neither independent nor identically distributed. So if we let the collection of random variables {Xt}t=0T\{X_t\}_{t=0}^T{Xt​}t=0T​ denote the data, a complete description is given by the joint distribution FX0,…,XTF_{X_0, \ldots, X_T}FX0​,…,XT​​. And that is impossible to estimate given we have a sample with a single point (N=1N = 1N=1).

To make the problem well-posed, we must impose some regularity conditions. For this we need the following definitions.

Let {Xt}\{X_t\}{Xt​} be a collection of time-indexed, real-valued random variables with the joint distribution

FX0,…,XT(x0,…,xT)=P(X0≤x0,…,XT≤xT). F_{X_0, \ldots, X_T}(x_0, \ldots, x_T) = \mathbb{P}(X_0 \leq x_0, \ldots, X_T \leq x_T).FX0​,…,XT​​(x0​,…,xT​)=P(X0​≤x0​,…,XT​≤xT​).

Def (Mean function): The mean function is defined as

μ(t)=E[Xt] \mu(t) = \mathbb{E}[X_t]μ(t)=E[Xt​]

for all ttt, if the expectations exist.

Def (Autocovariance function): The autocovariance function is defined as

γ(s,t)=E[(Xs−E[Xs])(Xt−E[Xt])] \gamma(s, t) = \mathbb{E}[(X_s - \mathbb{E}[X_s])(X_t - \mathbb{E}[X_t])]γ(s,t)=E[(Xs​−E[Xs​])(Xt​−E[Xt​])]

for all sss and ttt.

Def (Autocorrelation function): The autocorrelation function is defined as

ρ(s,t)=γ(s,t)γ(s,s)γ(t,t) \rho(s, t) = \frac{\gamma(s, t)}{\sqrt{\gamma(s, s)\gamma(t, t)}}ρ(s,t)=γ(s,s)γ(t,t)​γ(s,t)​

for all sss and ttt.

Now we can talk about the regularity conditions.

A series is strongly/strictly stationary if the joint distribution of any subcollection is the same as that of the shifted subcollection. Meaning the joint distribution depends only on the time differences rather than the actual times.

Def (Strong/Strict stationarity): A time series {Xt}t=0T\{X_t\}_{t=0}^T{Xt​}t=0T​ is said to be strongly/strictly stationary iff

FXt1,…,Xtk=FXt1+h,…,Xtk+h F_{X_{t_1}, \ldots, X_{t_k}} = F_{X_{t_1 + h}, \ldots, X_{t_k + h}}FXt1​​,…,Xtk​​​=FXt1​+h​,…,Xtk​+h​​

for all 0≤t1…≤tk≤T0 \leq t_1 \ldots \leq t_k \leq T0≤t1​…≤tk​≤T and h≥0h \geq 0h≥0.

Note that this means the XiX_iXi​'s are (marginally) identically distributed, but not that they're necessarily independent. For example, let X∼N(0,1){X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)}X∼N(0,1) and let Xk=(−1)kX{X_k = (-1)^kX}Xk​=(−1)kX for k∈Nk \in \mathbb{N}k∈N. Then XkX_kXk​'s are identically distributed but not independent, and the series is strongly stationary. So iid implies strong stationarity but it's not true the other way around.

This theoretical constraint is too strong to apply to the real world. Plus,it's hard to test. So we need a weaker, more practical condition.

Def (Weak stationarity): A time series {Xt}t=0T\{X_t\}_{t=0}^T{Xt​}t=0T​ is weakly stationary if the mean is constant and autocovariance depends only on the lag. So

μ(t)=μ \mu(t) = \muμ(t)=μ

for all ttt, and

γ(s,t)=γ(∣s−t∣) \gamma(s, t) = \gamma(|s - t|)γ(s,t)=γ(∣s−t∣)

for all s,ts, ts,t.

Instead of constraining the marginal distributions, we only control their first and second moments.

Note that strong stationarity implies weak stationarity. Also, when we talk about stationarity, it's weak stationarity in particular. Now let's consider a few classic examples.

Eg. (White Noise): Let WtW_tWt​ be independent random variables with mean 000 and variance σ2\sigma^2σ2. Then μ(t)=0\mu(t) = 0μ(t)=0 for all ttt and

γ(s,t)=E[WsWt]=E[Ws]E[Wt]={σ2,s=t0,s≠t.\begin{align*} \gamma(s, t) &= \mathbb{E}[W_sW_t] \\ &= \mathbb{E}[W_s]\mathbb{E}[W_t] \\ &= \begin{cases} \sigma^2, & s = t \\ 0, & s \neq t. \end{cases} \end{align*}γ(s,t)​=E[Ws​Wt​]=E[Ws​]E[Wt​]={σ2,0,​s=ts=t.​​

Clearly this series is (weakly) stationary. Instead, if we suppose that WtW_tWt​ are i.i.d. standard normal, then

fWt1,…,Wtk=∏fW0=fWt1+h,…,Wtk+h,\begin{align*} f_{W_{t_1}, \ldots, W_{t_k}} = \prod f_{W_0} = f_{W_{t_1 + h}, \ldots, W_{t_k + h}}, \end{align*}fWt1​​,…,Wtk​​​=∏fW0​​=fWt1​+h​,…,Wtk​+h​​,​

and the series becomes strongly stationary too.

Eg. (Moving Average) Let WtW_tWt​ be mean 000 variance σ2\sigma^2σ2 white noise variates and let Xt=Wt−1+Wt2X_t = \frac{W_{t-1} + W_t}{2}Xt​=2Wt−1​+Wt​​. Then

μ(t)=E[Xt]=12(E[Wt−1]+E[Wt])=0 \mu(t) = \mathbb{E}[X_t] = \frac{1}{2} (\mathbb{E}[W_{t-1}] + \mathbb{E}[W_t]) = 0μ(t)=E[Xt​]=21​(E[Wt−1​]+E[Wt​])=0

for all ttt, and

γ(s,t)={σ22,s=tσ24,∣s−t∣=10,∣s−t∣>1 \gamma(s, t) = \begin{cases} \frac{\sigma^2}{2}, & s = t \\ \frac{\sigma^2}{4}, & |s - t| = 1 \\ 0, & |s - t| > 1 \end{cases}γ(s,t)=⎩⎨⎧​2σ2​,4σ2​,0,​s=t∣s−t∣=1∣s−t∣>1​

for all sss, ttt. Since γ\gammaγ depends only on ∣s−t∣|s - t|∣s−t∣, this series is also stationary.

Eg. (Random Walk) Let WtW_tWt​ be mean 000 variance σ2\sigma^2σ2 white noise variates and let Xt=Xt−1+WtX_t = X_{t-1} + W_tXt​=Xt−1​+Wt​ with X0=0X_0 = 0X0​=0, which gives Xt=∑i=1tWiX_t = \sum_{i=1}^t W_iXt​=∑i=1t​Wi​. Then the mean function is

μ(t)=E[Xt]=0 \mu(t) = \mathbb{E}[X_t] = 0μ(t)=E[Xt​]=0

for all ttt, and

γ(s,t)=E[XsXt]=min⁡(s,t)σ2, \gamma(s, t) = \mathbb{E}[X_s X_t] = \min(s, t) \sigma^2,γ(s,t)=E[Xs​Xt​]=min(s,t)σ2,

for all sss, ttt. Since γ\gammaγ depends on both sss and ttt and not just their difference, this series is not weakly stationary. In fact in some sense this is a quintessential example of a non-stationary process since it's used to test data for stationarity — c.f. Augmented Dickey-Fuller test.

 

References

[1] Shumway, R. H., & Stoffer, D. S. (2017). Time Series Analysis and Its Applications: With R Examples (4th ed.). Springer, Cham, Switzerland.

entry.title: Introduction to Tree-based methods
entry.content:
Basic Idea

Let's consider the usual setup of a supervised learning problem with nnn data points and ppp predictors.

It's intuitive that points close to one another in the predictor space should have similar outputs. This is the idea behind kkk-NN (k-Nearest Neighbours). Take a distance metric, pick a kkk (how many nearest neighbours to look at), and decide how to predict (for example, by averaging or a majority vote).

Another reasonable claim is that there's a partition of the predictor space into regions such that points in a region have similar values of the response. This is similar to kkk-NN in that it's a local method, except that closeness isn't measured by distance from points but instead by belonging in a region. Tree-based methods take this approach.

More concretely, let's consider an out-of-sample point x\mathbf{x}x. The idea is (1) to partition the predictor space into regions R1,…,RmR_1, \ldots, R_mR1​,…,Rm​, (2) check which region x\mathbf{x}x belongs to, and then (3) guess the value based on this region. Steps (1) and (3) make use of the training data.

These regions can be arbitrary making the problem ill-posed. In fact, even if we only consider the partition into hyperrectangles, they can be staggered and hard to define. So we simplify the problem further by allowing only recursive binary partitions. I.e. any region can only be split further into two rectangular regions — the hyperrectangles are always neatly stacked.

Now, more choices need to be made based on the problem, so we consider regression and classification separately.

Regression

We want to answer: how to make the regions and how to predict values within them. In supervised learning this reduces to choosing a cost function and finding the parameters (the regions and guess values in this case) that minimize it on the observed data.

Suppose we already have the partition into regions, and for a region RjR_jRj​ we decide to predict the constant value cjc_jcj​ to minimize the mean squared error (MSE). Then our estimate of the underlying function is

f^(x)=∑j=1mcj1Rj(x),\begin{align*} \hat{f}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{j = 1}^{m}c_j \mathbf{1}_{R_j}(\mathbf{x}), \end{align*}f^​(x)=j=1∑m​cj​1Rj​​(x),​

and the MSE is

∑i=1n(yi−f^(xi))2.\begin{align*} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_i - \hat{f}(\mathbf{x}_i) \right)^2. \end{align*}i=1∑n​(yi​−f^​(xi​))2.​

Note that the MSE can be split into sums over the regions:

∑i=1n(yi−f^(xi))2=∑j=1m∑xi∈Rj(yi−f^(xi))2,\begin{align*} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_i - \hat{f}(\mathbf{x}_i) \right)^2 &= \sum_{j=1}^{m} \sum_{\mathbf{x}_i \in R_j}^{} \left(y_i - \hat{f}(\mathbf{x}_i) \right)^2, \end{align*}i=1∑n​(yi​−f^​(xi​))2​=j=1∑m​xi​∈Rj​∑​(yi​−f^​(xi​))2,​

and hence, the cjc_jcj​s that minimize the MSE are easily obtained by the mean of responses in the regions:

cj=1∣{xi∈Rj}∣∑xi∈Rjyi.\begin{align*} c_j = \frac{1}{|{\{\mathbf{x}_i \in R_j\}|}} \sum_{\mathbf{x}_i \in R_j} y_i \text{.} \end{align*}cj​=∣{xi​∈Rj​}∣1​xi​∈Rj​∑​yi​.​

It turns out that finding the best possible partition that gives the lowest MSE is also computationally infeasible. So we take a greedy, iterative approach. At each step, we look at all possible splits for all possible predictors in a region, and choose the predictor and split that gives the largest reduction in MSE. The two new regions are added to the queue of all regions and the process can continue (in principle) till there's only one data point left in each region.

Pros and cons

Although this algorithm is easy to implement and gives interpretable decision trees, they have a high variance and generalize poorly. I.e. the fully-grown trees overfit the training data and have low predictive power.

At the level of individual trees this is tackled by specifying growth constraints, or by cost complexity pruning. But there are ways to combine multiple weak trees to get a strong estimator that are much more effective — namely bagging and boosting.

 

References

[1] Hastie, Trevor, Robert Tibshirani, and Jerome Friedman. The Elements of Statistical Learning: Data Mining, Inference, and Prediction. 2nd ed. Springer Series in Statistics. New York: Springer, 2009. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-84858-7.

[2] James, Gareth, Daniela Witten, Trevor Hastie, and Robert Tibshirani. An Introduction to Statistical Learning: with Applications in Python. 2nd ed. Springer Texts in Statistics. Cham: Springer, 2023. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-38747-0.

entry.title: Computing Bond Yields
entry.summary: using numerical methods like Bisection and Newton's Method.
entry.content:
All bonds are not created equal. There may be many differences: The borrowing party may be the US government, or the World Bank, or a company like Apple. The borrowed amount could be in millions of euros, or billions of dollars. It could be paid back all at the end of 10 years, or partly every month for 30 years. The lender could have additional options, or the borrower more restrictions.

How can we then compare different bonds? The answer is: using Mathematics.

Keeping only the most necessary and useful properties, and ignoring the rest: A bond is simply a promise to pay back certain amounts at certain times, and it can be traded in the market for a price.

Now, consider a bond: let FFF be its face value, CCC be the coupon payment, TTT be the time periods to maturity and PPP be the market price. The yield to maturity rrr is defined as the interest rate that solves the equation:

P=∑t=1TC(1+r)t+F(1+r)T.\begin{align*} P &= \sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{C}{(1+r)^t} + \frac{F}{(1+r)^T}. \tag*{(1)} \end{align*}P​=t=1∑T​(1+r)tC​+(1+r)TF​.​(1)​

It is the discount rate which equates the present value of the bond's cash flows to its market price. This assumes that (1) the bond is held to maturity, and (2) the issuer makes the coupon and principal payments as promised.

To think of rrr as the return on the bond, it is also assumed that (3) the coupons are (or can be) reinvested at the yield:

P(1+r)T=∑t=1TC(1+r)T−t+F.\begin{align*} P(1+r)^T &= \sum_{t=1}^{T} C(1+r)^{T-t} + F. \tag*{(2)} \end{align*}P(1+r)T​=t=1∑T​C(1+r)T−t+F.​(2)​

The left hand side is the future value of an investment of PPP at the yield rrr for TTT periods, and the right hand side is the future value of the cash flows from the bond with reinvestment of coupons at the yield.

At the cost of a few assumptions, a single meaningful number rrr can be used to compare very different bonds.

What's left now is actually solving for rrr. Not long after staring at the equations, you might realize the good news and the bad news. There are no weird sin⁡\sinsin, cos⁡\coscos or log⁡\loglog terms, it's only a polynomial equation. But, unlike the quadratics from high school, it has no general closed-form solution (formula).

So, we turn to Numerical Analysis. The idea is to keep trying values of rrr such that: (1) every attempt is better than the previous one, (2) ultimately the LHS and the RHS are very close (if not equal), and (3) all this happens reasonably fast.

Two such methods are the Bisection Method and the Newton's Method.

But before diving into them, note that solving for rrr in equation (1) is the same as solving for rrr in

f(r)=∑t=1TC(1+r)t+F(1+r)T−P=0.\begin{align*} f(r) &= \sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{C}{(1+r)^t} + \frac{F}{(1+r)^T} - P \\ &= 0. \tag*{(3)} \end{align*}f(r)​=t=1∑T​(1+r)tC​+(1+r)TF​−P=0.​(3)​

Also, this f(r)f(r)f(r) is decreasing in rrr. It looks like:

Bisection Method

In spirit, it's just like binary search. Start with r1r_1r1​ and r2r_2r2​ such that f(r1)>0f(r_1) > 0f(r1​)>0 and f(r2)<0f(r_2) < 0f(r2​)<0. Then the interval [r1,r2][r_1, r_2][r1​,r2​] definitely contains the root. Guessing initial values could be challenging, but in this case, r1=0r_1 = 0r1​=0 and r2=1r_2 = 1r2​=1 are easy choices.

  1. Now, check the sign of f(r1+r22)f\left(\frac{r_1 + r_2}{2}\right)f(2r1​+r2​​).
  2. If it's positive, set r1:=r1+r22r_1:=\frac{r_1 + r_2}{2}r1​:=2r1​+r2​​; if it's negative, set r2:=r1+r22r_2:=\frac{r_1 + r_2}{2}r2​:=2r1​+r2​​.
  3. Repeat steps 1 and 2 till ∣f(r1+r22)∣<ϵ\left|f\left(\frac{r_1 + r_2}{2}\right)\right| < \epsilon​f(2r1​+r2​​)​<ϵ.

Here, ϵ\epsilonϵ is an error tolerance parameter decided by the user.

Newton's Method

Since f′′(r)>0f''(r) > 0f′′(r)>0, f(r)f(r)f(r) is a convex function. The Newton's method exploits this artfully. Start with an arbitrary value of r=r0r=r_0r=r0​, then

  1. Get the equation of the tangent to fff at rnr_nrn​: y=f(rn)+f′(rn)(r−rn){y = f(r_n) + f'(r_n)(r - r_n)}y=f(rn​)+f′(rn​)(r−rn​).
  2. Get the r-intercept of this line; set y:=0y := 0y:=0, then rn+1=rn−f(rn)f′(rn){r_{n+1} = r_n - \frac{f(r_n)}{f'(r_n)}}rn+1​=rn​−f′(rn​)f(rn​)​.
  3. Repeat steps 1 and 2 with r=rn+1r = r_{n+1}r=rn+1​ till ∣f(rn)∣<ϵ\left|f(r_n)\right| < \epsilon∣f(rn​)∣<ϵ.

Again, ϵ\epsilonϵ is an error tolerance parameter.

Newton's method is much faster (quadratic convergence) than bisection and hence used in practice:

You can play around with the implementations using numanpy, the code for which is here. You can also look at the bond yield computation in this Jupyter Notebook.
